title: Inflammation, muscle damage and postrace physical activity following a mountain ultramarathon
authors: Martinez-Navarro I, Collado E, Hernando C, Hernando B, Hernando C
journal: The Journal of Sports Medicine and Physical Fitness
population: 34 athletes (29 men, 5 women) in a 118-km mountain ultramarathon; blood before, immediately after, day 3 and day 7; accelerometer activity in the week after
findings: CK was significantly higher in faster runners at 3 days postrace (d = 1.17); LDH was higher in faster runners at 3 and 7 days (d = 1.01 and d = 1.05).
Race time correlated with CK and LDH at day 3 (rs = -0.41 and -0.52) and at day 7 (rs = -0.36 and -0.46): faster races went with higher damage markers.

Postrace physical activity levels did not differ between faster and slower runners, and activity was not associated with muscle damage and inflammation recovery, except light-intensity activity and CRP at day 3 (rs = -0.40).

Authors conclude race time had a higher influence on muscle damage recovery than postrace physical activity intensity; inflammatory activity takes longer to normalise than muscle damage and is not related to race time.
limitations: Only days 3 and 7 sampled; the abstract does not state whether markers had normalised by day 7; activity was observational, not an intervention; n = 34 with 5 women.
implications: Faster finishers had higher CK and LDH at days 3 and 7, so the hold could scale with effort and pace and not distance alone; the engine lacks a good effort input, so keep this as a documented caveat.

Light activity in the week after a mountain ultra was not linked to worse marker recovery (observational), which is consistent with walking and very easy activity being compatible with a no-running hold.
CRP and inflammation take longer to normalise than CK, supporting a graded second week.

verification.notes: Crossref and PubMed give a five-author list (Martinez-Navarro, Collado, Hernando C, Hernando B, Hernando C); the record's list was wrong and is corrected. Abstract re-read from PubMed and Europe PMC (PMID 33555667): d values, rs values and conclusions match. The 'finish pace' wording in an implication was softened to what the abstract states (race time).
